title: Special Edition: The Shield Hero's Valentine's Day [2]
text: “Heh heh heh, well then, next up… it’s my turn, isn’t it?”

The accessory merchant stood up and asked me. Seriously, why do you guys come across as such obvious villains? I guess it might be a bit awkward for me—the ringleader—to point that out, though. What if people start thinking I’m one of you too?
“The accessory designs proposed by the Shield Hero are showing signs of becoming a trend. Your skill in incorporating superstitions to create trendy styles—I’m truly in awe.”

Drawing on our experiences on Cal Mira Island, the accessory merchant has partnered with me to create various superstitions. For example, “prayer for business success”—we’ve collaborated with the Guild of Righteous Thieves to create superstitions like, “If you hang this accessory from your carriage, you won’t run into bandits.” However, he even added the caveat that it’s less effective if you’re engaged in shady business practices.

Even with underhanded tactics like this, the profits are substantial. Surprisingly, people really do value this kind of superstition. Even folks who don’t usually believe in gods will visit shrines during New Year’s or participate in festivals just to buy amulets.

We set the duration of the superstition’s effect at one month, ensuring that items without new designs are targeted for theft. By creating these superstitions, many merchants are drawn to come buy these accessories. Then, after investigating the backgrounds of the merchants who bought them, the Robin Hood Guild takes action. In other words, we’re essentially making them say, “I’m a merchant—go ahead and investigate me.” After all, the very fact that they’re willingly buying something like this means there’s a high chance they’re involved in shady business they can’t talk about.
I’m a total villain myself, but what about those accessory merchants? They’re also spreading rumors among the underground guilds and running the show in those circles.
“So? What kind of ore are you using for the new accessories? Ideally, something regionally exclusive that’s currently worth next to nothing.”
“Right. The current candidates are—”

And so, they’re selecting rare, worthless ores found within my territory—ones that aren’t worth a penny—and crafting them into accessories. The trick is that these cheap accessories, simply by bestowing a jinx, miraculously turn into gold. This is alchemy—though not in the traditional sense.
Though it’s the dark underbelly of a terribly sinister jinx. Anyway, that wraps up the jewelry merchant’s story.
“Is that it?”
“Shield Hero. Yes.”
The slave trader raised his hand.
“What is it? Didn’t you finish your part?”
“Yes. I’d forgotten about a request from Zeltoble. Yes.”
“So?”
“It concerns the Filolials being raised in your territory, Hero.”

Currently, Filolial races are booming in Zeltoble. The special Filolials raised on my estate are overwhelmingly outclassing the established champions and sweeping past them. Trainers and gambling operators occasionally come to my estate and ask around—probably talking to Motoyasu or someone like that. Well, it’s practically cheating. There’s no way they could replicate it. So I have a pretty good idea of what’s going on.
“We’ve received an inquiry asking if it would be okay to hold a separate race category, since the Filolials raised by the Hero have been performing so exceptionally well.”
“I figured as much.”

No matter how you look at it, there’s no way ordinary Filolials could stand a chance against those mutated ones called Queens and Kings. On top of that, they can even disguise themselves as ordinary Filolials. The screening process is practically nonexistent. It seems they’ve swept every prize race, so this outcome was inevitable.
“You’d rather just keep them in a separate category, wouldn’t you?”
“As expected of the Hero—you’re absolutely right. Yes.”
“What can you do? Besides, it’ll be the talk of the town—people will get to enjoy races that are even faster than those with ordinary Filolials. If you send us our cut, I’ll grant permission.”
“Thank you very much. We’d like to have our entire clan come together to express our gratitude to the Shield Hero.”
The entire slave trader clan!? I seem to recall seeing an uncle who looked exactly like this guy! That means it’s a family business—a bunch of lookalikes might be swarming all over me!
“Y-you guys must be busy, too. S-sorry, but I’ll just take the thought.”
“That’s a shame. Yes.”
Anyway, the meeting went off without a hitch.
The Robin Hood-type was listening to our meeting with a look of frustration. When the slave trader and the jewelry merchant eventually left, I felt the tension in his shoulders ease slightly.
“What’s wrong?”
“Nah, nothing.”
“Really?”

Come to think of it, what was this guy’s name again? Was it Rowdy? I don’t really remember. He did tell me his name once when I called him “Rogue,” but since we aren’t on the kind of terms where we openly call each other by name, he hasn’t left much of an impression on me.
“Well, if nothing’s wrong, that’s fine.”
As I muttered that, the Rogue spoke up, as if it had taken him a while to find the words.
“It’s not exactly that…”
“Hm?”
“I was just thinking that this Rogue Guild has really grown…”
“Ah, so that’s what you mean.”

Before the waves stopped… that was before the Phoenix War, so more than half a year ago. Can you even call it just half a year? I’m amazed it’s grown this much in such a short time. As it turns out, now that the world has become more peaceful than it was during the era of constant warfare, it has become a vital organization and expanded rapidly.
“It’s all been going so smoothly… and it’s growing so fast that I’m starting to feel uneasy.”
“I see.”
“I’m in a position now where I have to provide for my comrades, and as the boss, I’m doing my best… or at least I think I am, but I just can’t shake this anxiety.”

Hmm… I can understand that. Before the waves, no matter how much I prepared, I couldn’t shake my anxiety. Even when I thought I’d created the best possible situation, I couldn’t emerge unscathed, and there were always sacrifices.

It’s the same with my status as a hero who saved the world. People come out in droves to praise me and shower me with words of gratitude. It’s not just this world—the folks from Glass’s world are the same. Everyone—absolutely everyone—places strong gratitude and high expectations on us, the heroes who saved the world. The era of staining the earth with blood has finally come to an end. Since we put an end to such a dark age, I suppose it can’t be helped.
It doesn’t feel bad to be relied upon, but the weight bearing down on me is correspondingly heavy.

I wouldn’t say it’s exactly the same, but I understand how he feels. Even I have my own anxieties about whether I’ll be able to make it from here on out. I was just a college student to begin with. When it comes to fighting, I can manage with the power of the shield, but the world ahead won’t be all about violence. I’ve relied on the shield’s power until now, but that will gradually become unnecessary. When that happens, what a college student—who’s nothing more than a “Shield Hero who saved the world”—can do will be limited accordingly.

Now that I’ve remained in this world, I hold the title of Grand Duke and own lands befitting that position. And with vast lands come, naturally, the duty to protect the people who live there. Being a hero doesn’t just mean charging head-on at monsters and shielding those behind you. As your status and power grow, your capabilities expand—but so do your responsibilities.

If you rise to power, you’ll get rich, eat plenty of delicious food, and be able to build a harem. It’d be fine if it were that simple, but at least in my case, there are plenty of troublesome responsibilities that come with it. There’s no way I wouldn’t feel anxious about that.
But that’s precisely why I can offer advice.

“Don’t let your subordinates see you looking too anxious, okay? There are probably as many as the stars in the sky who’d try to pull off some foolish coup d’état and take over this place at a moment like that.”
“That’s a bit of a hard pill to swallow, isn’t it?”
The Shadow, who had seen off the slave trader and the jewelry merchant, joined the conversation. What’s this? Does even the Shadow—the nation’s dark underbelly—understand this?

“Since we, too, are infiltrating the Guild of Righteous Thieves, we monitor our subordinates’ actions closely. Just the other day, we disposed of someone who tried and failed to stage a coup against the boss, didn’t we?”
So even here, there was a struggle—survival of the fittest, or rather, a battle with fools craving the top spot. Well, it’d be strange if there weren’t.
“Well, as for foolish fools or those who defy me, I’ll just have my men subtly ambush their carriages. Disposing of them is easy.”

Those who admire this Robin Hood are utterly captivated by his ability to discern dangerous situations. Even if they suspected his true identity—that he’s secretly connected to dangerous adversaries—they probably wouldn’t bother to verify it. Even if they wanted to verify it, it’s nearly impossible given the presence of a shadow here with keen detection skills and the ability to lie in wait. It’s too difficult for a mere thief.

Besides, this “righteous thief” has currently raised his level to 150. The “40 barrier” was removed because the system unlocked Class Ups for people who became vulnerable due to the waves, allowing them to protect themselves. In other words, 100 is the current limit for ordinary people.

Of course, now that the Dragon Hourglass has been returned to controlled status, Class Ups aren’t so easy anymore. But because—even if only temporarily—it was a situation where anyone could do it, there were quite a few thieves who’d surpassed Level 40.

However, this Robin Hood pushed them even further, breaking through that limit to grant them greater strength. He’s made sure his subordinates don’t reveal his actual Level. He’s made them view him as a terrifyingly strong boss whom they admire. In fact, combat sense aside, it’s possible to just power through with a high level.
“I know. It’s just… I’m scared.”
“Scared?”

“Slave hunting wasn’t exactly rare a year ago, was it? Trying to set rules for something like that, or scheming to control the Dark Guild—it’s just way too big a scale. What are we going to do if we lose?!”
“We’ll silence them physically.”

I think we can do it now. If the Black Guild were to send assassins after us, labeling us as dangerous elements, we’d threaten to storm Zeltoble with all the Heroes and crush the Black Guild itself. Ultimately, a minimum level of power is necessary for negotiation. Justice without power is powerless, after all.

If war could be eliminated through discussion alone, life wouldn’t be so hard. Even in that war-free era—the modern-day Japan I came from—there were still conflicts. There was that troublesome kind of war called “economic war,” where there are no visible casualties. Ultimately, even in that case, if it didn’t suit the major powers, they’d impose tariffs and other restrictions; and if tariffs didn’t work, it would have escalated into a physical war.
“What!?”

“Anyway, don’t panic. If anything happens, we’ve got arrangements in place to back you up. You’re the boss here, but you’re also under my command as the Shield Hero. As long as you do what you’re supposed to do, I’ll protect you.”
“I see… Got it.”
Even as he said that, the Robin Hood’s face remained gloomy.
“…Or was your old life as a thief actually more carefree?”
The Robin Hood nodded at my question.
“It was easy just being used. If something went wrong, I could just run away. Thinking only of myself, pursuing my own pleasure. I sometimes miss those days—that’s all there was to it.”
“Do you want to go back? Or rather, do you want to get a legitimate job?”

If that’s the case, I’d consider letting him go. In this day and age, it’s not that hard to make a living if you have a legitimate job. If he doesn’t want to do it from the bottom of his heart, forcing him to won’t do any good. Well, I did bribe him with a so-called katsu-don, but… Still, the Robin Hood-style thief shook his head, his troubled expression unchanged.
“No, sure, I stole it, but when I give it to people in need and they thank me… well, it makes me happy. I don’t actually mind the work itself.”
“I see.”
I suppose it’s fine if he finds his own sense of fulfillment in it? But I guess that also means the pressure is intense.

“The family I left behind in the countryside… they think I’m doing good things… but I guess this is actually a bad thing. Still, it’s also a good thing. I don’t think they’ll understand, but it’s rewarding.”
“That’s what a Robin Hood-type is. A Robin Hood-type is someone who does good deeds through bad means.”
Sometimes even good people can’t do good deeds. After all, people who are rotten to the core are the ones who slip through the cracks of the rules to do bad things.
…Is he talking about me? I don’t know.

That’s why Robin Hood-types punish villains who can’t be brought to justice openly and help the weak. In our case, it’s a little different, but it’s also true that there are people being saved because of it. Still, wrong is wrong. That fact doesn’t change. But if I can’t ease this guy’s anxiety, it’s a problem for me, too. Hmm. Maybe I’ll stimulate the thrill of those who operate behind the scenes.
“You should know this, but even if the world is saved, there will always be villains. This will continue—whether ten years, a hundred years, or a thousand years pass… as long as there are people.”

“Many of you guys probably turned to thievery because you were struggling to make ends meet, but there are countless others who keep doing bad things even when they have more than enough to eat, wear, and live in.”
“Yeah.”
“Among those people are some whom even we heroes—who saved the world—can’t do anything about.”

That’s the truth. It’s quite difficult to judge someone simply because they’re doing bad things. One wrong step, and it’s the beginning of a dictatorship. And the future that unfolds that way becomes a dystopia.
“You’re the only one who can judge those parasites of the world—those hopeless scum.”
“Just… me?”
To be able to do something even the heroes everyone praises can’t do—that must be a different kind of thrill.
“That’s right. You, the Robin Hood, are the one who can judge the villains that even the heroes can only stand by and watch.”
This might not even be much of a consolation, though.
“Well, do your best. As long as you don’t screw up too badly, I’ll back you up.”
“Ah, yeah!”

It seemed to me that the Righteous Thief’s expression had improved a bit since earlier. Well, I guess that’s about it. Now, time to head back to the village. Just as I was thinking that, the Righteous Thief spoke up.
“Shield Hero, come to think of it—”
